claims.claim: title: "Over 800,000 crimes a year, 0 records"
claims.source: HM Inspectorate of Constabulary, Crime-recording: making the victim count (hmic2014.txt extraction)
claims.passage: Over 800,000 crimes reported to the police have gone unrecorded each year.7 This represents an under-recording of 19 percent.
claims.notes: A fair compression of para 1.16 (the crimes got no record), though footnote 7 says the figure is an estimate extrapolated from the 81 percent audit rate, which the title does not signal.

claims.claim: status: "the National Statistics designation removed in January 2014 has not come back"
claims.source: Office for Statistics Regulation, The quality of police recorded crime statistics for England and Wales, 16 May 2024
claims.passage: The police recorded crime statistics for England and Wales are published as official statistics, not accredited official statistics . We removed their National Statistics accreditation in 2014 following an assessment which found evidence that the quality and consistency of the underlying data may not be reliable.
claims.notes: Sourced only to May 2024; the present-tense 'has not come back' on a page published October 2026 rests on no listed source, though a search found no later reaccreditation.

claims.claim: status: "as of May 2024 the survey was not accredited either"
claims.source: Office for Statistics Regulation, 16 May 2024 review
claims.passage: Currently, the CSEW statistics are published as official statistics, not accredited official statistics, due to challenges with response rates that affect the quality of the estimates. We will be reviewing the accreditation status of the CSEW statistics in 2024.
claims.notes: True as dated, but the same paragraph announced a 2024 review, and OSR's letter of 17 October 2024 (Ed Humpherson to Jen Woolford) says: 'We are pleased to confirm the reaccreditation of the CSEW estimates'; set next to 'has not come back' in the present tense, the line implies a status that is 2 years out of date.

claims.claim: teaser: "2 official counts, and the 19% of reported crime 1 of them never recorded"
claims.source: HMIC 2014 para 1.16; ONS YE March 2016 bulletin
claims.passage: This represents an under-recording of 19 percent.
claims.notes: 19% matches para 1.16, and ONS describes '2 main sources' of crime statistics.

claims.claim: ledger: National Statistics designation removed, January 2014
claims.source: UK Statistics Authority, Assessment Report 268 (ar268.txt); OSR publication page
claims.passage: Assessment Report 268  January 2014 ... 1.2.5  Therefore, the Authority has removed the National Statistics designation from statistics based on recorded crime data
claims.notes: The cover date, para 1.2.5 and the OSR page date ('15 January 2014') agree.

claims.claim: ledger: reported crimes unrecorded each year, over 800,000
claims.passage: Over 800,000 crimes reported to the police have gone unrecorded each year.
claims.notes: Verbatim match; footnote 7 calls it an estimate.

claims.claim: ledger: under-recording of reported crime 19%
claims.passage: This represents an under-recording of 19 percent.
claims.notes: Exact.

claims.claim: ledger: under-recording violence against the person / sexual offences 33% / 26%
claims.passage: The problem is greatest for victims of violence against the person and sexual offences, where the under-recording rates are 33 percent and 26 percent respectively.
claims.notes: Exact, and in the right order.

claims.claim: ledger: no-crime decisions reviewed / incorrect 3,246 / 664
claims.passage: Of the 3,246 decisions to cancel, or no-crime8, a crime record that we reviewed, 664 were incorrect.
claims.notes: Exact.

claims.claim: ledger: crime records classified correctly 96%
claims.passage: Our audit showed that 96 percent of crime records reviewed were classified correctly, either at the time of initial recording or subsequently.
claims.notes: Exact.

claims.claim: ledger: recording accuracy 2014 / end of 2021 to 2022 inspections 80.5% / 92.4%
claims.passage: HMICFRS's inspections estimate that crime recording accuracy nationally has improved in the last ten years , from 80.5% ( ± 2.0% ) of all crimes (excluding fraud) in 2014 to 92. 4 % ( ± 0.3% ) at the end of the 2021 to 20 22 inspection programme, a statistically significant change.
claims.notes: Exact; the live fetch confirmed the same figures.

claims.claim: ledgerNote: "HMIC's 81% recorded and the OSR's 80.5% are the same 2014 audit, rounded differently."
claims.passage: provide a national rate for the accuracy of police recording of 81 percent.43 ... 43 With a confidence interval of (+ / - 2 percent).
claims.notes: The two are consistent (same year, both exclude fraud, both have a 2-point interval), but no source says OSR's 80.5% is HMIC's 81% unrounded; this is the draft's own inference.

claims.claim: verdict Fraud detected: "relatively little. HMIC looked for \"dishonest manipulation\" and found \"relatively little\". It found under-recording of 19% and called it \"wholly unacceptable\"."
claims.passage: We looked for hard evidence of improper practices (such as dishonest manipulation) in crime-recording as a result of performance pressure, and approached those who told us that it was going on, but relatively little was found. However, in and since the inspection, a number of forces accepted that undue performance pressure had adversely affected crime-recording in the past, and the culture of chasing targets as ends in themselves had distorted crime-recording decisions.
claims.notes: Each quote is verbatim, but 'looked for "dishonest manipulation"' shortens 'hard evidence of improper practices (such as ...)', and the row drops the very next sentence, in which forces accepted that target culture had distorted recording.

claims.claim: verdict Rules broken: the Commons committee found misrecording "ingrained, including within senior leadership". The Statistics Authority removed the designation.
claims.passage: The attitudes and behaviour which lead to the misrecording of crime have become ingrained, including within senior leadership.
claims.notes: Verbatim and correctly attributed to the committee.

claims.claim: verdict Usefulness: police-recorded crime is "generally, not a reliable measure of trends in crime"
claims.source: ONS, Crime in England and Wales: year ending March 2016 (fetched live)
claims.passage: Police recorded crime is, generally, not a reliable measure of trends in crime, since it is prone to changes in recording practices and police activity
claims.notes: Verbatim.

claims.claim: verdictNote: The Statistics Authority set the condition for the designation's return in 2014: evidence that the underlying data and the audit procedures are sufficient.
claims.passage: until such time that ONS, working with the Home Office, HMIC or other appropriate bodies, is able to demonstrate that the quality of the underlying data, and the robustness of the ongoing audit and quality assurance procedures, are sufficient to support its production of statistics based on recorded crime data to a level of quality that meets users' needs.
claims.notes: A fair paraphrase.

claims.claim: verdictNote: The inspectorate's own figures put recording accuracy up from 80.5% to 92.4%.
claims.passage: HMICFRS's inspections estimate that crime recording accuracy nationally has improved in the last ten years , from 80.5% ( ± 2.0% )
claims.notes: OSR attributes the estimates to HMICFRS inspections.

claims.claim: verdictNote: The regulator's response, 10 years after the removal, was a review it called the first step towards reaccreditation.
claims.passage: This review is the first step towards the statistics being considered for reaccreditation.
claims.notes: January 2014 to 16 May 2024 is 10 years 4 months, and OSR itself says 'the last ten years'; 'response' implies a causal link the source does not state, and 'towards reaccreditation' drops 'being considered for' (minor).

claims.claim: verdictNote: the survey, the count ONS calls the better measure of trends, was not accredited either, "due to challenges with response rates"
claims.passage: Currently, the CSEW statistics are published as official statistics, not accredited official statistics, due to challenges with response rates that affect the quality of the estimates.
claims.notes: Accurate as of May 2024 (the sentence is past tense); see id 20 for what happened next.

claims.claim: verdictNote: "As of May 2024, England and Wales had 2 official crime counts and no accredited one."
claims.source: OSR 2024 (listed); OSR letter 17 October 2024 (not listed, fetched to test currency)
claims.passage: We are pleased to confirm the reaccreditation of the CSEW estimates, ... starting from the next release of the statistics on 24 October 2024.
claims.notes: True for May 2024, but the CSEW was reaccredited 5 months later; ending the verdict on 'no accredited one' in an exhibit published in October 2026 leaves a reader with a status that ended in October 2024.

claims.claim: body: ONS says the survey "provides the better measure of trends"
claims.passage: For the population and offence types it covers, the CSEW provides the better measure of trends on a consistent basis over time.
claims.notes: Verbatim fragment; the scope qualifier is dropped, which is acceptable.

claims.claim: body: police-recorded crime "is, generally, not a reliable measure of trends in crime", being "prone to changes in recording practices and police activity"
claims.passage: Police recorded crime is, generally, not a reliable measure of trends in crime, since it is prone to changes in recording practices and police activity (for example, a proactive operation on weapon offences)
claims.notes: Verbatim.

claims.claim: body: In January 2014 the UKSA cited "accumulating evidence that suggests the underlying data on crimes recorded by the police may not be reliable"
claims.passage: that there is accumulating evidence that suggests the underlying data on crimes recorded by the police may not be reliable.
claims.notes: Verbatim.

claims.claim: body: removed the National Statistics designation from statistics based on recorded crime data ... until ONS could show the data and the audit procedures "are sufficient"
claims.passage: the Authority has removed the National Statistics designation from statistics based on recorded crime data10 until such time that ONS ... is able to demonstrate that the quality of the underlying data, and the robustness of the ongoing audit and quality assurance procedures, are sufficient
claims.notes: Accurate.

claims.claim: body: In November 2014 HMIC reported on its audit of every force.
claims.passage: November 2014 ... Our in-force audit and inspection work was carried out between February and August 2014 and covered all 43 Home Office-funded police forces.
claims.notes: The cover date and the coverage both match.

claims.claim: body: It found 81% of reported crime being recorded.
claims.passage: This estimate has been calculated by applying our audit finding that 81 percent of reported crime is being recorded
claims.notes: Verbatim basis.

claims.claim: body quote: "Over 800,000 crimes reported to the police have gone unrecorded each year. This represents an under-recording of 19 percent." plus 33% / 26%
claims.passage: Over 800,000 crimes reported to the police have gone unrecorded each year.7 This represents an under-recording of 19 percent. The problem is greatest for victims of violence against the person and sexual offences, where the under-recording rates are 33 percent and 26 percent respectively.
claims.notes: Verbatim, with the footnote marker dropped.

claims.claim: body: Of 3,246 decisions to cancel a crime record, 664 were incorrect, including over 200 rapes.
claims.passage: Of the 3,246 decisions to cancel, or no-crime8, a crime record that we reviewed, 664 were incorrect. These included over 200 rapes and more than 250 crimes of violence against the person.
claims.notes: Accurate.

claims.claim: body: 96% of the records it reviewed were classified correctly.
claims.passage: Our audit showed that 96 percent of crime records reviewed were classified correctly
claims.notes: Accurate.

claims.claim: body: The Commons Public Administration Select Committee reported in April 2014.
claims.passage: HC 760 Published on 9 April 2014
claims.notes: Matches the title page.

claims.claim: body: Its chair had been contacted by "a serving police officer, PC James Patrick, acting as a whistleblower, who had serious concerns about the validity of crime statistics."
claims.passage: 2. The Chair of PASC was contacted by a serving police officer, PC James Patrick, acting as a whistleblower, who had serious concerns about the validity of crime statistics.
claims.notes: Verbatim and attributed to the committee, so the individual has an institutional paper trail.

claims.claim: body: committee summary "The attitudes and behaviour which lead to the misrecording of crime have become ingrained, including within senior leadership. This leads to the subordination of data integrity to target-chasing."
claims.passage: The attitudes and behaviour which lead to the misrecording of crime have become ingrained, including within senior leadership. This leads to the subordination of data integrity to target-chasing.
claims.notes: Verbatim.

claims.claim: body: It deprecated targets "in the strongest possible terms" and called the end of regular external audit in 2007 "a mistake".
claims.passage: We deprecate the use of targets in the strongest possible terms. ... The cessation of regular external audit of police force crime recording in 2007 was a mistake.
claims.notes: Verbatim.

claims.claim: body: HMIC called the failure to record "wholly unacceptable".
claims.passage: This failure to record such a significant proportion of reported crime is wholly unacceptable.
claims.notes: Verbatim.

claims.claim: body: It had looked for "hard evidence of improper practices (such as dishonest manipulation)", and "relatively little was found."
claims.passage: We looked for hard evidence of improper practices (such as dishonest manipulation) in crime-recording as a result of performance pressure, and approached those who told us that it was going on, but relatively little was found.
claims.notes: Both fragments are verbatim; the following 'However' sentence about forces accepting distortion is omitted (see id 13).

claims.claim: body: In the year ending March 2016 the survey fell 6% and police-recorded crime rose 8%.
claims.source: ONS YE March 2016 bulletin; Figure 1 data (main-session extraction, BRIEF S6)
claims.passage: 6% fewer than in the previous survey year (6.8 million). ... The police recorded 4.5 million offences in the year ending March 2016, an annual rise of 8%.
claims.notes: The bulletin states both; the S6 values give 6334/6764 = -6.4% and 4513.964/4174.239 = +8.1%, consistent.

claims.claim: body and source: ONS said "most of the latest rise is thought to be due to improved crime recording practices and processes"
claims.source: ONS YE March 2016 bulletin, main points (fetched live)
claims.passage: However, this series is not considered a reliable indicator of trends in crime; most of the latest rise is thought to be due to improved crime recording practices and processes leading to a greater proportion of reports of crime being recorded in the last year than in the previous year.
claims.notes: Verbatim (one of the main-session edits, confirmed).

claims.claim: body: Inspections later put recording accuracy at 80.5% in 2014 and 92.4% at the end of the 2021 to 2022 programme, "a statistically significant change".
claims.passage: from 80.5% ( ± 2.0% ) of all crimes (excluding fraud) in 2014 to 92. 4 % ( ± 0.3% ) at the end of the 2021 to 20 22 inspection programme, a statistically significant change.
claims.notes: Verbatim.

claims.claim: body: In May 2024 OSR still listed PRC as "official statistics, not accredited official statistics", and called its review "the first step towards the statistics being considered for reaccreditation."
claims.passage: The police recorded crime statistics for England and Wales are published as official statistics, not accredited official statistics . ... This review is the first step towards the statistics being considered for reaccreditation.
claims.notes: Verbatim; the page date is 16 May 2024.

claims.claim: body: The same review gave the survey the same status, "due to challenges with response rates".
claims.passage: Currently, the CSEW statistics are published as official statistics, not accredited official statistics, due to challenges with response rates that affect the quality of the estimates. We will be reviewing the accreditation status of the CSEW statistics in 2024.
claims.notes: 'Gave' is loose: the review reported an existing status (OSR suspended it in 2022), and it flagged a 2024 review that ended in reaccreditation on 17 October 2024.

claims.claim: HMIC source entry: "the 81% recording rate for the 12 months ending July 2014 (footnote 7)"
claims.passage: applying our audit finding that 81 percent of reported crime is being recorded to police-recorded crime figures for the 12-month period ending July 2014.
claims.notes: July 2014 is the period of the police figures the 81% was applied to, not of the 81% itself, and HMIC's own footnote 33 gives 'the 12-month period ending March 2014' for the same estimate.

claims.claim: HMIC source entry: the inspection covered all 43 Home Office-funded police forces
claims.passage: Our in-force audit and inspection work was carried out between February and August 2014 and covered all 43 Home Office-funded police forces.
claims.notes: Verbatim (main-session edit, confirmed).

claims.claim: HMIC source entry: the 'relatively little' quote is located in 'summary and conclusions'
claims.passage: Summary and conclusions
claims.notes: The passage sits in the unnumbered text after para 1.19 under the 'Summary and conclusions' heading (repeated in section 7); its paragraph number cannot be confirmed because -layout scrambled the numbering (1.20 to 1.30).

claims.claim: ONS Figure 1 source: CSEW 6,764 to 6,334 (down 6%), police-recorded crime 4,174 to 4,514 (up 8%)
claims.source: ONS Figure 1 xls (main-session extraction, BRIEF S6)
claims.notes: I could not read the xls myself (binary); against the main session's sheet extraction the rounding and the -6.4% / +8.1% arithmetic both hold.

claims.claim: ONS Figure 1 footnote: "Police recorded crime data are not designated as National Statistics."
claims.source: ONS Figure 1 xls (main-session extraction, BRIEF S6)
claims.passage: (1) "Police recorded crime data are not designated as National Statistics."
claims.notes: Rests on the main-session extraction only; the live xls fetch returned binary.

claims.claim: UKSA source entry: published 15 January 2014
claims.passage: 15 January 2014
claims.notes: Page date confirmed.

claims.claim: PASC source entry: Thirteenth Report of Session 2013-14, HC 760, 9 April 2014; para 1 January 2014 removal
claims.passage: Thirteenth Report of Session 2013-14 ... HC 760 Published on 9 April 2014 ... the UK Statistics Authority (UKSA) decided in January 2014 to strip PRC data of its designation as National Statistics.
claims.notes: All details match the title page and para 1.
